Environmental groups spent Tuesday at the Michigan Capitol pressing lawmakers to regulate data centers, saying they're worried about the facilities' effects on water, air and the health of nearby communities.

"The missing ingredient is action — so that's really what we're focused on," said Marta Johnson, a legislative and political organizer with Sierra Club Michigan.

Sierra Club Michigan was joined in Lansing by Clean Water Action, the Michigan Climate Action Network and the Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition.

"The overall concern is really that we don't have any regulations right now on these," Johnson said. She said the groups want to protect groundwater and surface water, and to guard against pollution from diesel generators and gas plants, along with noise that she said "can impact human health."

Some state rules already touch the industry. In November 2025, the Michigan Public Service Commission adopted a rate structure requiring data centers in Consumers Energy's territory to sign long-term power contracts and pay for the grid infrastructure needed to serve them, CBS Detroit reported. In July, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer asked data center companies to sign a 10-point pledge on costs, environmental permits and hiring, and called on the Legislature to write those guardrails into law.

Chris Gilmer-Hill, with the Michigan Environmental Justice Coalition, said he heard a wide range of opinions on data centers from lawmakers.

"But there's a real and growing consensus that we need something real moving on from what we have now," Gilmer-Hill said. "We're seeing more and more folks at the very top echoing our grassroots call for a moratorium."

text:
US-based Montauk Renewables has opened a $200m agricultural biogas facility in North Carolina, converting swine waste into renewable natural gas (RNG or biogas) and electricity.

The facility, developed at the site of a former Bay Valley Foods Distribution Centre, captures methane from swine manure and converts it into renewable energy products, while also producing biochar as a co-product.

The project is supported by long-term agreements with more than 80 farming locations across Sampson County. These agreements provide access to around 415,000 hog spaces targeted during the project’s first phase of development.

“As of the end of August, we have entered into long-term agreements with over 80 separate farming locations, providing us access to more than 415,000 of the hog spaces we are targeting for our first phase of development,” said Sean McClain, CEO of Montauk Renewables.

Montauk specialises in capturing biogas from agricultural and landfill sources and converting it into RNG or electricity. The company currently operates 14 projects across the US, with further developments underway in California, Idaho, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas.

The North Carolina facility also produces biochar from the waste conversion process. The solid material can be used as a soil amendment, with applications including improving nutrient and water retention.

“The biochar produced here will also improve nutrient and water retention, supporting healthier soil and stronger crop yields,” said Senator Brent Jackson, a Sampson County farmer and agricultural policy leader in North Carolina’s General Assembly.

The facility forms part of Montauk’s wider strategy of developing agricultural biogas projects in areas with concentrated livestock production.

North Carolina has approximately 42,000 farms across eight million acres, with agriculture contributing more than $100bn to the state’s economy, according to information released alongside the facility’s opening.

US biogas growth

The opening comes as the US biogas sector continues to develop a large pool of potential projects. Data from the American Biogas Council (ABC), reported by gasworld in April, identified more than 17,000 additional biogas systems that could potentially be deployed across the country.

Nearly 2,600 biogas capture facilities are already operating in the US, with 52% of biogas output used for electricity generation and 44% upgraded to RNG in 2025.

The expansion of RNG production could also create additional opportunities for biogenic CO2 recovery.

Data from the RNG Coalition indicates that around 474 RNG facilities are currently operational across North America, with the potential to recover approximately 2.25 million tonnes of CO2 annually. A further 440 facilities in development could add another 2.1 million tonnes per year of potential recoverable CO2.

text:
Leaders of three poultry and feed industry organizations said sustainability must be weighed against trade-offs, workforce needs and disease threats during a CEO panel at the 2026 Poultry Sustainability & Welfare Summit on Sept. 22.

The summit was hosted by the U.S. Roundtable for Sustainable Poultry and Eggs and the International Poultry Welfare Alliance. The panelists were Nath Morris, president of USPOULTRY; Megan Provost, chief operating officer of the American Feed Industry Association; and Chad Gregory, president and CEO of United Egg Producers.

Progress by another name

Morris, who has spent 40 years in the poultry industry, said the gains the industry has made over decades amount to sustainability, whatever they were called at the time.

"The progress may have been called something other than sustainability, but it was progress through genetics, through feeding structures, through management, through housing," Morris said. "Everything like that has helped with sustainability."

Words matter

Asked how much the label itself matters, Morris said the language the industry uses shapes how the public sees it.

"Words are important. If you look back on the history of a lot of the processes we go through, we call our broiler plants slaughter plants, we say debeaking chickens, we talk about culling," he said. "Some of the words that we're using create a negative perception."

"We've got to do some repairing of our image to attract more people to come in and work in the industry," Morris said.

Trade-offs and a systems approach

Morris cautioned that changes seen as welfare improvements, such as cage-free housing for layers and slow-growing broilers, can carry environmental costs. Slower growth means poorer feed conversion and more land and housing to produce the same amount of meat, he said.

"Unintended consequences — it's the same as trade-offs," he said. "Whether it's passing laws or changing programs, you've got to think through: If we do this, then what's going to happen? I don't think there's enough thought that goes into that from either politicians or some businesses."

Provost said that is why AFIA views sustainability as a system rather than a checklist.

"I think too often in the sustainability space, outsiders coming in will focus on one piece of that broader puzzle, and I think that really is a disservice to what we're doing as a sector," Provost said. "It's not a collection of individual metrics. It's an overall system that we need to be managing."

She pointed to carbon as an example.

"If you set goals for carbon, you have to think about how that might have some impacts on land use. Maybe it's going to take more acres to do the same kind of work," she said. "Because it is a system, there are going to be trade-offs along the way."

A shifting priority for egg farmers

Gregory, who has been with UEP for 29 years, said sustainability's standing among egg producers rises and falls with customer demands.

"Is it one of the top two or three biggest issues for U.S. egg farmers today? No," he said. "Was it four or five years ago? Yes, it probably was."

"I love the quote from Mike Tyson: Everybody's got a plan until you get punched in the face," Gregory said. "Another saying that I think applies to sustainability is: By the time you need friends, it's too late to make them."

Is sustainability sustainable?

Gregory said he has long questioned whether sustainability is sustainable itself. He cited the Coalition for Sustainable Egg Supply, a two-year research project led by McDonald's and Cargill that compared conventional cage, enriched colony and cage-free housing on commercial farms.

"At the end of those two years, cage-free was the worst of the three systems for the environment," he said. "And yet those same customers that funded that two-year commercial, on-farm study said, 'We're going to go cage-free.' And I couldn't believe it."

Responding to Chavonda Jacobs-Young, former U.S. Department of Agriculture undersecretary and chief scientist, who provided the meeting’s keynote address, who had asked whether farmers can continue to make a living, Gregory offered a different question.

"I think for the U.S. egg industry, maybe the more appropriate question is: Do I want to keep doing this?" he said.

"It isn't just about people, planet and profits," Gregory said. "It's about a lot of things."

He said that is why UEP values the roundtable's diverse membership.

"If UEP were to put together a sustainability platform on our own, we wouldn't include all the different buckets and stakeholders that are in this room," he said. "So, when this becomes a top three issue for the U.S. egg industry again, we will be ready, because we're members of the roundtable."

Gregory said that whatever it is called, sustainability comes down to keeping farms in business.

"All the components that go into a good sustainability program are the exact same components that go into running a business that's successful and can be passed from generation to generation," he said.

People and bird flu

Asked to name the No. 1 issue the industry must get right, Morris said it is people.

"We're down to six poultry science departments in the U.S.," he said. "We've got to find ways to attract people into this industry, and we can't just depend on the six poultry science departments. We need people who understand artificial intelligence. We need robotics engineering, HR folks, communicators to tell our story."

Gregory agreed that workers are important but said the most urgent threat for egg producers is highly pathogenic avian influenza. "We need a vaccine," he said. "The U.S. egg industry needs a vaccine, and we obviously don't want to hurt trade for the chicken industry."

Food security and resiliency

Gregory said sustainability also extends to food security. He recalled a speaker at a soybean industry meeting 20 years ago who predicted the U.S. might one day ship grain to China and import the resulting meat, eggs and milk.

"If that happens, all they've got to do is just shut the spigot off for a couple of weeks, and we're starving to death," Gregory said. "Sustainability is a big, big conversation."

Provost said supply chain resiliency is the sustainability-related issue drawing the most interest from the feed industry.

"When we're talking about not being able to get some of those key additives, some of those vitamins and amino acids, that has real impacts on animal welfare, on animal health, on food security more broadly," she said.

She said a recent study by the Institute for Feed Education and Research found how dependent the industry is "on a handful of countries, and one country in particular, for our vitamin and amino acid supply."

Despite the challenges, Gregory said poultry is well positioned with consumers who are paying new attention to where their food comes from.

"We've got a great story to tell, and we've got a great product that they want to eat," he said.

text:
Texas signed two rare earth mineral leases to expand the Round Top Project and reduce dependence on China, Land Commissioner Dawn Buckingham said.

“Texas has the land, the resources, and the workforce to lead America into a new era of critical mineral production,” said Buckingham. “For too long, communist China has controlled resources essential to our economy and national security. We are changing that right here in the Lone Star State.”

The leases expand the Round Top Project, the nation’s most advanced heavy rare earth development. The project contains 16 of the 17 rare earth elements and provides a strategic source of dysprosium and terbium, which are vital for high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, and missile guidance systems. Round Top plans to begin commercial production in 2028.

“These resources are essential to national defense, advanced manufacturing, and energy technologies. Yet for decades, the United States has depended heavily on foreign adversaries for their supply,” noted the General Land Office.

Covering 1,000 acres in Hudspeth County, the new leases advance Texas’ efforts to establish its first dedicated rare earth mining district.

“Round Top Mountain has already put Texas on the map for domestic rare earth and critical mineral development, with USA Rare Earth serving as the founding partner in advancing this vision. These new leases with El Paso Minerals Corp. build on that momentum and demonstrate what the responsible development of Texas state land can accomplish,” stated Buckingham.

Alex Moyes, senior vice president of mining and separation for USA Rare Earth, praised Buckingham’s leadership. “Her support for responsible resource development and policies that encourage investment have helped position Texas and USA Rare Earth as a leader in critical minerals and rare earth development. We are grateful for her partnership and for her commitment to strengthening American and Allies supply chains, creating jobs, and advancing long-term economic growth while helping secure the resources essential to our nation’s future.”

Cesar Gonzalez, CEO of El Paso Minerals, said, “Our existing private leases, together with these new GLO leases, give El Paso Minerals the largest land position in the district, which we believe has the potential to supply a meaningful percentage of U.S. heavy rare earth demand and eventually eliminate America’s dependence on China. We are now preparing to drill our primary target and are excited to be working with Commissioner Buckingham and the Texas GLO.”

Earlier this year, Commissioner Buckingham allotted up to $1.6 billion for the Round Top’s mine-to-magnet supply chain to “keep America’s mineral resources under American control—from the ground to the finished product.”

title: Cirba Solutions, GM pilot focused on closing EV battery recycling loop
description:
Through a strategic collaboration between automaker General Motors (GM), battery recycler Cirba Solutions and other partners, the parties say they have successfully completed a closed-loop electric vehicle (EV) battery recycling pilot.
According to Charlotte, North Carolina-based Cirba Solutions, the pilot involved using materials recovered from end-of-life GM EV battery packs to produce new battery cells—marking the first GM EV batteries made with cathode active material (CAM) containing 100 percent-recycled nickel, cobalt and manganese.
Closing the loop Detroit-based GM has partnered with Cirba Solutions to disassemble and process end-of-life EV battery packs as part of the pilot.

text:
Through a strategic collaboration between automaker General Motors (GM), battery recycler Cirba Solutions and other partners, the parties say they have successfully completed a closed-loop electric vehicle (EV) battery recycling pilot.

According to Charlotte, North Carolina-based Cirba Solutions, the pilot involved using materials recovered from end-of-life GM EV battery packs to produce new battery cells—marking the first GM EV batteries made with cathode active material (CAM) containing 100 percent-recycled nickel, cobalt and manganese.

Closing the loop

Detroit-based GM has partnered with Cirba Solutions to disassemble and process end-of-life EV battery packs as part of the pilot. Cirba Solutions says the EV battery materials were transported to its lithium-ion recycling and recovery facility in Lancaster, Ohio, to be processed into black mass.

The battery recycler says that recovering the critical minerals through recycling is the first step, adding that minerals such as cobalt, nickel and manganese help determine a battery’s performance. Before any recycled materials from end-of-life batteries can go into manufacturing new EV cells, those materials must meet the same standards as virgin minerals, and Cirba Solutions says this was successfully achieved through a partnership to further refine its premium-quality black mass, validating its performance, to produce new recycled-content CAMs.

Cirba Solutions says its work with GM has produced new EV battery cells using recycled CAM through Ultium Cells, a joint venture between GM and South Korea-based LG Energy Solution. GM manufacturing teams assembled the cells into battery modules and packs at its Factory Zero in Detroit and Spring Hill assembly plant in Tennessee. This month, GM’s first battery cells containing recycled-content CAM rolled off the line.

“This pilot shows that the value of an EV battery can extend well beyond its first life, and that strong partnerships across the battery ecosystem are essential to building a more circular, resilient future for battery technology,” says Melissa Flaherty, director of sustainable EV battery ecosystem at GM.

Enhancing domestic supply chains

According to research cited by Cirba Solutions, nearly 14 million EV batteries are projected to reach their end of life globally by 2040, and the global demand for lithium-ion batteries is expected to reach approximately 4.2-6.8 terawatt-hours annually over the next decade. The recyclers says its program with GM demonstrates that recycled material can be recovered and used in new EV batteries.

Additionally, Cirba Solution says increasing domestic processing capabilities opens opportunities for advancing closed-loop models for all battery formats, including EVs, energy storage systems, data centers, consumer devices and more.

“Battery recycling is an important, intersecting component across the battery supply chain, and this program effectively demonstrates the value that recycling end-of-life batteries brings to creating a closed-loop supply of critical minerals,” Cirba Solutions President and CEO David Klanecky says. “The global battery supply chain is an interconnected network of innovative and collaborative organizations—and engaging in partnerships like this with GM shows us how this work can truly strengthen our supply chains, manufacturing, global competitiveness and national security.”

Cirba Solutions adds that through partnerships similar to its work with GM, the recovery and reuse of critical minerals can help support lower-cost batteries over time, leave positive impacts on the environment, reduce reliance on newly mined materials, advance manufacturing and, ultimately, strengthen supply chain resilience.

Salem — Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll today joined students, faculty, staff and community partners at her alma mater, Salem State University, to celebrate major progress on two clean energy projects that are transforming how the campus is heated, cooled and powered.

The university’s “Closing the Loop” event marked the installation of a new geothermal loop that will provide efficient heating and cooling to campus buildings while reducing reliance on fossil fuels. The event also highlighted a new solar canopy over the College Drive parking lot.

“Our public colleges and universities are showing what it looks like to invest in more efficient public buildings, creating jobs and serving students and communities for years to come,” said Governor Maura Healey. “These projects will modernize Salem State’s campus, making it a healthier place for students and lowering long-term operating costs. These are the kinds of investments that move Massachusetts toward a cleaner energy future.”

“I’m proud to see my alma mater leading by example and making investments that students will see and feel across campus,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll ’89, ’22H. “This work means more efficient buildings, cleaner energy and modern infrastructure that will serve Salem State for decades. It’s a great example of what we can accomplish when the state and our public colleges work together.”

The geothermal project, undertaken in partnership with the Massachusetts Division of Capital Asset Management and Maintenance (DCAMM), represents a transformative investment in Salem State’s campus infrastructure. The system will circulate low-temperature hot water and chilled water to efficiently heat and cool to campus facilities, including the new addition to Meier Hall and the renovated Horace Mann Building on Salem State’s North Campus. The Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources (DOER) provided $3.5 million in funding for the geothermal system and new solar canopy.

As part of the celebration, attendees were invited to sign a section of geothermal piping before it becomes part of the campus system.

“This geothermal loop is more than an infrastructure project—it is an investment in the future of Salem State and a tangible expression of our commitment to environmental stewardship,” said Salem State University President John Keenan. “Our students deserve a campus that reflects the future we are preparing them to lead. Through projects like this, we are reducing our environmental impact, modernizing our campus and demonstrating what is possible when the university, the Commonwealth and our partners work together toward a shared vision.”

The event also highlighted Salem State’s new solar canopy over the College Drive parking lot, expanding renewable energy generation on campus. Together, the geothermal loop and solar canopy will help reduce greenhouse gas emissions, modernize campus infrastructure and improve long-term resilience.

“Decarbonizing the Commonwealth’s buildings requires ambitious projects, strong partnerships and a willingness to rethink how we heat, cool and power our facilities,” said DCAMM Commissioner Adam Baacke. “Salem State’s geothermal loop is an excellent example of that work in action. DCAMM is proud to partner with the university to deliver modern, sustainable infrastructure that reduces fossil fuel use, improves campus resilience, lessens ongoing maintenance burdens, and likely reduces long-term costs benefitting students and the Commonwealth for decades.”

“Salem State has already shown how innovative clean energy projects benefit its students, staff and community, and we’re thrilled to celebrate the campus’ new geothermal system and solar canopy,” said Energy Resources Commissioner Elizabeth Mahony. “Projects like these address energy and climate challenges at the same time by lowering energy costs and reducing harmful emissions, and they also create local workforce and economic opportunities. We value our partnerships with DCAMM and Massachusetts’ public colleges and universities to forward projects that improve energy affordability and public health in Massachusetts.”

The projects are part of Salem State’s broader work with the state to modernize campus infrastructure and reduce its environmental impact. For example, two completed clean-energy projects conducted by SSU and the state include comprehensive LED lighting upgrades throughout the campus and execution of a 3-phase Energy Performance Contract focusing on HVAC upgrades, boiler replacements, ice rink efficiency, and EMS upgrades. Through its partnerships with DCAMM and DOER, the university is investing in cleaner energy systems that support its academic mission and position the campus for the future.

Governor Healey has also proposed the BRIGHT Act, which is a $2.5 billion investment to modernize Massachusetts’ public higher education infrastructure while creating nearly 20,000 construction-related jobs.

text:
Story by Connor Foote

DURHAM, NC — Bryce Brooks has spent most of her professional life asking other people for their trash. She’s managed waste for Durham Central Park for more than a decade, and in that time founded two different organizations that aim to ease some of the stressors in the recycling process.

One of those, The ReCollective, was inaugurated in 2022 by Brooks and business partner Kevin Younge. At the time, Brooks had been focusing on managing waste for commercial businesses, but after connecting with Younge through North Carolina’s Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ), the pair began to lay the groundwork for a service which would supplement the other side of waste management — traditional curbside recycling.

“With residences, you have to worry about residential compliance and having a system that is easy for everyone to do,” Brooks said. “Having a system that makes sense to a lot of people is difficult to kind of conceive of because what we’ve been raised on, in curbside recycling, in traditional recycling services, is single-stream.”

Single-stream recycling means that all the different recyclable materials on a truck’s route get mixed together before being divvied up at what they call a sortation center. But many recyclable materials cannot be properly handled through single-stream service. Each municipality has different rules about what can and can’t be recycled, and often what they won’t accept is still recyclable.

To ease what is often a confusing municipal service, The ReCollective’s vans set out each month to pick up much of this hard-to-recycle material from more than 400 households on routes spanning from Garner to Greensboro.

They return with canvas bags full of plastic film, styrofoam and crinkly packaging — practically everything that your municipal curbside service won’t accept. Inside its Durham warehouse, mountains of plastic bags cover the cinderblock walls, yards of textiles are packed into large cardboard bins and various school supplies await delivery to classrooms. Some materials get baled together and shipped off to processing facilities. Others are donated or sold directly for reuse.

“We want everyone to try and consume less, to do less Amazon shopping, to do more circular economy and to be more thoughtful,” Brooks said. “We offer a way to do that while still living your life and meeting your waste where you are.”

The ReCollective has met more and more waste during its four years of life, adding full-time and part-time employees to manage a rapidly expanding customer base as well as a growing list of accepted materials. The business operates on a subscription model, and customers pay from $19 to $51 for Brooks’ team to bring them closer to the circular economy. Services like The ReCollective are popping up across the country to supplement the circular economy and combat misconceptions about waste management.

The vast majority of recycling in the U.S. is carried out through county or municipal contracts, which face a variety of structural barriers to better results. Much of the material coming in will gum up grinders and incinerators or just isn’t dense enough to justify energy and transportation costs.

The hard truth is that recycling is often an inefficient and flawed method of waste management — in short, it’s a business. Yes, there are significant environmental aspects that are indivisible from the process, but recyclers also need to make money. If the price isn’t right on transporting, storing and reforming waste, a material will exit the economy for good.

In contrast to a linear economic model, in which materials leave a factory and eventually find a permanent home in landfills, by the roadside or in the ocean, the aim of a circular economic model is to generate as much reuse as possible — to get the stuff you throw in the green bin back circulating in the economy.

“They want volume, so a lot of times with plastic recyclers, they are not willing to handle individual residential volumes because it’s more work on the front end,” Brooks said. “Because we are taking so many different materials, we can aggregate and make sure that we are producing the volumes that the plastic recyclers want.”

Recycling entrepreneur Mimi Wu noted that there are many considerations when choosing a material for a product. Wu worked in the southeast Asian country of Myanmar to develop the post-use supply chain for dirty plastic bags, where she found monetary barriers to effective recycling.

“It’s really not a ‘valuable’ product at the end of the day,” Wu noted. “People don’t really want to use it. It’s so much cheaper to just make virgin plastic that it’s almost not even worth collecting it.”

The process of recycling really begins when R&D and marketing departments decide how to present and package their product. Typically, companies aren’t willing to sacrifice their color schemes in favor of using recycled material, especially in cases where recycled material costs more than virgin material. A November 2024 study from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis found that those cases are common — recycled plastic cost $0.72 per pound in North America, whereas virgin plastic cost $0.58.

Another issue is transportation. Many hard-to-recycle materials are low-density, which translates to inefficient space usage in transportation and storage. Without expensive in-residence machinery to compact these materials, the unit cost is too high for municipal recyclers. Part of The ReCollective’s expansion has been enabled by its ability to consolidate and ship off these low-density materials at a rate that makes logistical sense.

At this point, some might be inclined to agree with a recent thought trend: recycling just isn’t worth the effort. It seems to fit nicely into the narrative that all pollution is just the fault of large corporations, and that consumers don’t really bear the burden of proof.

Yet this isn’t actually the case. Brooks, Wu and Matt James of North Carolina’s Recycling Business Assistance Center (RBAC) all agree that most consumers are a long way from recycling efficiently.

“Roughly 21% of all material that is sent to a material recovery facility, a sortation plant, is contamination, and that is a cost right off the top,” James said.

Despite structural issues like material type, infrastructure and profitability, James said the biggest issue facing recycling is household sorting. When done improperly, consumers either contaminate or throw away what is otherwise perfectly good material.

“Our goal at DEQ is to make sure that folks have just as easy accessibility to recycling as they do to throwing something away in a landfill,” James said. “And a problem is that we are throwing a lot of recoverable material away in our landfills, taking up valuable landfill space.”

A not-insignificant portion of what ends up in landfills is actually quite recyclable. Even in Orange County, one of the most effective recycling districts in the state, a fifth of landfill material would have been accepted by curbside recycling.

When Orange County resident and UNC public health student Connor Bost moved closer to campus ahead of the fall semester, he noticed his roommates weren’t as particular about recycling as he was. To help them recycle better, he pointed them toward Orange County Solid Waste’s A-Z waste guide.

“It does take a lot of deliberate effort,” Bost said. “You have to take the time to maybe educate yourself, at least on a baseline level, about what can and can’t be recycled, what kind of procedures need to be taken in order to recycle something. Like if I have a bottle that I want to recycle, but it’s got food waste on the inside, that’s not eligible for recycling. I need to rinse that out first, and so it’s kind of knowing those guidelines and steps that need to be taken.”

There are significant structural limitations to growing the circular economy. In an ideal world, we would produce as little virgin material as possible, and live by the three Rs (reduce, reuse, recycle) otherwise. But Brooks said the most impactful solution is also the easiest: educating ourselves about what can and cannot be recycled.

“I don’t think we should feel bad about the trash that we’re creating,” Brooks said. “I don’t think we should have be ashamed, but we can’t look away from it, and I think that that’s the biggest point that I would make: that when we look away from it, we don’t actually understand that what we’re doing with curbside recycling in the city is making it worse overall for landfills and city recycling.”

Waste management doesn’t start nor end with consumers. Other people decide which materials to use and manage most of the operations that actually get them back into circulation. But while consumers wait for corporations to become more environmentally conscious and for municipalities to upgrade waste management infrastructure, experts say consumers still have the most power in deciding if waste belongs to the linear or the circular economy.

Key in this, Brooks noted, is recycling with integrity — knowing your limits in order to confidently make your impact. And if after consuming responsibly and consulting your resources you’re still struggling to find a home for yards of bubble wrap or a drawer full of used vapes, maybe give The ReCollective a call.

text:
NEW YORK, NY — As the U.S. federal government continues its retreat from global climate efforts, governors and mayors representing America’s top state- and city-led climate action coalitions — the U.S. Climate Alliance and Climate Mayors — came together today at Climate Week NYC to announce a new joint partnership that supercharges non-federal climate collaboration, reinforcing the strength and durability of American climate leadership.

The new agreement was announced during an event featuring leaders of both organizations, including Climate Mayors chair Boise Mayor Lauren McLean and Alliance co-chair Delaware Governor Matt Meyer, as well as Alliance executive committee member New York Governor Kathy Hochul, who provided remarks via video message. Alliance co-chair Washington Governor Bob Ferguson was originally scheduled to participate, but was unable to attend due to flight disruptions in the Northeast.

The Alliance is a bipartisan coalition of 24 governors — representing approximately 60 percent of the U.S. economy and 55 percent of the U.S. population — sustaining America’s fight against climate change with bold, state-led action.

“We’re facing a hostile federal administration, intent on taking us backward,” said Alliance co-chair and Washington Governor Ferguson. “The governors and mayors in our partnership are not going to let that happen. Together, we are a force. By working together, we can continue to make meaningful progress on climate, clean energy, electrification, and more.”

“The partnership we’re announcing today is built on a simple idea: When governors and mayors get together, we get things done. We don’t make promises, we make plans, and we turn those plans into real progress for real people,” said Alliance co-chair Delaware Governor Matt Meyer. “Let’s be clear about what we’re fighting for — we’re reducing pollution, we’re building resilience, we’re expanding clean energy. We’re leveraging the technologies of tomorrow for generations to come and we’re doing these things because they improve people’s lives.”

Climate Mayors is the nation’s largest and most diverse coalition of city leaders — representing more than 350 mayors across 47 states — committed to advancing climate action that lowers costs, cuts pollution and strengthens communities.

“Our progress is not happening in isolation. It is the result of cities and states working together, sharing what works, and bringing proven solutions to deliver cleaner air, stronger communities, greater affordability, and a more resilient future for our residents,” said Climate Mayors Chair and Boise Mayor Lauren McLean. “We are accelerating the solutions already working in our cities and states, turning local innovation into national momentum, and demonstrating what’s possible when leaders across levels of government work together.”

Despite federal rollbacks and attempts to undermine the irrefutable science underpinning climate action, America’s states and cities retain significant authority to continue developing, adopting, and implementing solutions to climate change. In fact, states and cities in the U.S. have long worked together to advance policies addressing climate change, serving as laboratories of innovation for impactful and scalable climate solutions.

These solutions have already delivered meaningful progress in communities across the country. Since 2005, the Alliance’s members have collectively cut electricity sector emissions by 44 percent and quadrupled electricity generated by wind and solar, while growing their economies by 37 percent.

In Climate Mayors cities, as the collective population grew 1.2 percent and collective economies grew 11.3 percent between 2019 and 2024, fossil fuel consumption per person fell 3.5 percent — a clear sign that cities are decoupling economic growth from fossil fuel use. This shift translated into $27.2 billion less fossil fuel spending over five years in Climate Mayors cities. Lower fuel use is putting money back into household budgets, saving people on average $1,000 a year.

Through this new partnership, the Alliance and Climate Mayors will work to achieve a series of shared objectives, including to:

Accelerate the deployment of clean energy and technologies across U.S. states and cities, including to lower household energy costs, grow the economy, and bolster U.S. energy security.

Reduce greenhouse gas pollution consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement.

Build resilience to the impacts of climate change.

Support the creation of good-paying jobs in climate and clean energy fields.

Promote consistency and minimize disruption across federal administrations and fluctuations in federal policy priorities.

Leverage opportunities for collective action to drive policy innovation, transform markets, and lay the foundation for future federal action.

Share U.S. state and city progress with the global community.

Together, the coalitions will advance bold and sustainable climate change solutions through peer learning, intergovernmental exchanges, and shared resource development. The cross-sectoral work will focus on clean electricity and energy affordability, healthy buildings and communities, transportation decarbonization, climate resilience, building and supporting a climate-ready workforce, and more.

These areas of engagement build on the already strong foundation of state and local climate partnership over the past two years. This includes the Alliance and Climate Mayors spotlighting U.S. climate progress together at London Climate Action Week and leading a delegation of leaders to COP30 and the Local Leaders Forum in Brazil, in partnership with America Is All In. The coalitions also joined forces to encourage Americans to take advantage of cost-saving federal clean energy tax credits before they expired, following passage of President Trump’s H.R. 1. The coalitions will build on this partnership later this year at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

Today’s event was part of America Is All In’s Local to Global Exchange, which brought together local, state, and global leaders to highlight how they’re collaboratively deploying ambitious climate solutions that create tangible community benefits — from lowering energy costs to reducing air pollution.

“After so many years in government, there is one thing I know to be true: real and lasting progress always comes from the bottom up. The more local leaders are supported and empowered across the United States, the faster and farther we’ll go, which is why I’m thrilled to see these two great organizations working together to lead our clean energy revolution,” said America Is All In Chair and former White House National Climate Advisor and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Gina McCarthy. “States and cities are laser-focused on tackling ‘kitchen table’ issues and grabbing every opportunity they can to invest in technologies that lower costs, cut pollution, deliver healthier homes, and create good-paying union jobs to protect their communities.”

text:
By Ernest Scheyder

Sept 22 (Reuters) – US metals refining startup Nth Cycle has signed a $1 billion offtake agreement with Glencore to supply the commodities giant with lithium and other critical minerals extracted from recycled batteries, a deal that comes ahead of a planned public listing later this year.

The ​10-year deal is among the largest in the US battery recycling sector as companies and governments ‌race to secure domestic sources of critical minerals needed for electric vehicle batteries and other clean energy technologies.

The agreement, which Reuters is first to report, was signed on Tuesday at Glencore’s New York offices at a time when critical minerals are expected to be an area of focus at this week’s United Nations General Assembly.

Massachusetts-based Nth Cycle’s technology uses an electrochemical process to extract ‌critical ​minerals from electronic waste, shredded batteries or mined rock.

As part of the ⁠deal, Glencore will sell Nth Cycle ⁠roughly 24,000 metric tons per year of shredded battery parts known as black mass for it to process, essentially supplying it the feedstock from which to extract the minerals.

Nth Cycle will then process that black mass and supply Glencore with lithium carbonate and a nickel-rich material known as mixed hydroxide product for ​10 years. The exact volume will depend on the percentage of minerals in the black mass, which can vary depending on battery chemistry.

The deal value reflects metals pricing as of the second quarter of this ⁠year, the companies said.

Nth Cycle, which in August received a $100 million ⁠grant from the US Department of Energy, is planning to build a commercial facility ​somewhere in the US Southeast to process the minerals for Glencore as well as commodities trader Trafigura under the terms ​of a similar deal announced in March.

The location of the commercial facility is set to ‌be announced later this year with operations beginning by 2029. That is a shift from earlier this year when Nth Cycle planned to build the facility in South Carolina and open by 2028.

The company now says it doubled the planned size of its facility due to the Energy Department grant and is now searching for a ⁠larger site.

“This is a true strategic partnership between the companies, and really just accelerates the overall critical minerals market here in the US,” said Megan O’Connor, Nth Cycle’s CEO.

Glencore, which is a large marketer of black mass and ⁠last year bought the assets of ‌bankrupt battery recycler Li-Cycle, said it aims to “help close the loop in the ⁠supply of critical minerals for our US customers.”

PUBLIC LISTING EXPECTED BY END OF ​YEAR

The Glencore ‌agreement comes after Nth Cycle said in July it would go public through ​a merger with ⁠special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Kensington Capital Acquisition, a deal that values the company at $585 million.

Nth Cycle had canceled a planned Series C funding round earlier this year, a move O’Connor said was tied to a desire for more funding from the public listing.

“We decided that going public was what we needed,” said O’Connor. “I’d be surprised if you met a company that wasn’t looking at multiple fundraising options at the same time.”

(Reporting by Ernest Scheyder; Editing by ​Chris Reese and Sanjeev Miglani)

text:
Clean energy jobs drop for first time since pandemic crisis, second since tracking began in 2015

WASHINGTON – The U.S clean energy workforce fell by nearly 37,000 jobs last year, according to new analysis by the national nonpartisan business group E2. Overall, more than 3.5 million Americans still work in clean energy—the largest employment sector in the energy industry.

The analysis of recently released U.S. Department of Energy data reflects the impacts of the first year of the Trump administration’s policy actions against clean energy, including the July 2025 passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which rolled back tax incentives and programs for clean energy manufacturing, generation, and job creation. The numbers released today represent the first time since the height of the COVID-19 pandemic that companies cut clean energy jobs.

Three of the largest clean energy sectors – renewables, energy efficiency and clean vehicles – saw job losses in 2025, with losses felt in 35 states. The biggest impacts were felt in states with the largest clean energy workforces, with California alone losing almost 21,000 jobs.

The analysis was released during E2 events at Climate Week in New York.

Following is a statement from Bob Keefe, executive director of E2:

“These numbers paint a clear picture of what is happening after a year of project cancellations and federal policy attacks. When federal leaders play politics, American workers and our economy pay the price.”

Michael Timberlake, director of research for E2 said:

“America’s clean energy jobs boom didn’t just slow in 2025—it went into reverse. After four consecutive years of strong growth, the industry lost nearly 37,000 jobs—its first decline since the pandemic.”

The data represents an early look at E2’s upcoming 11th annual Clean Jobs America analysis. The full report—which will include expanded findings on clean energy jobs across every state, county, industry, and all 47 clean energy sub-technologies—is expected to be released later this October.

The employment decline follows the sharp reversal in project activity that E2 began tracking in 2025. According to E2’s Clean Economy Works project tracker, companies canceled or downsized 142 clean energy manufacturing, generation and storage projects in response to abrupt federal policy rollbacks last year.

To download the analysis memo with table totals by state and sector, click here.

To arrange interviews with Bob Keefe or Michael Timberlake, contact Ana Little-Saña (alittlesana@e2.org) or Alex Frank (afrank@hastingsgroupmedia.com).

The full Clean Jobs America 2026, with complete state, county, subsector, per capita, and historical data will be released later this October, including an updated interactive county and state map. Contact Ana Little-Saña (alittlesana@e2.org) or Alex Frank (afrank@hastingsgroupmedia.com) if you would like to receive an early notice of that report.

—

About E2’s Analysis

Employment figures are based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy’s 2026 U.S. Energy & Employment Report (USEER), with prior-year comparisons from E2’s Clean Jobs America 2025. This latest data coincides with employment estimates at the end of Q4 2025. USEER counts jobs rather than unique workers and uses survey-based estimates; totals may not sum exactly because of rounding.

text:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has repealed most of the Biden administration’s 2024 “Carbon Pollution Standards, Greenhouse Gas Requirements for Coal- and Gas-fired Power Plants,” which is expected to save $310.4 billion over 20 years, lower electricity prices, and increase coal production. The decision would remove requirements that future and existing fossil fuel power plants implement carbon dioxide emissions-reduction technologies that do not exist commercially. The EPA also has proposed rescinding all remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants and a separate measure that could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants.

According to industry groups, the rollback will help preserve coal-fired power plants, protect grid reliability and prevent higher costs amid rising demand from increased electrification, data centers and advanced manufacturing. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Energy Secretary Chris Wright announced the rule changes at a G20 ministerial meeting on “energy abundance” in Houston. EPA will hold a public hearing for the proposal 15 days after publication of the action in the Federal Register as well as a 45-day public comment period. The rule is expected to be challenged in court.

The separate rule EPA proposed concludes emissions from fossil-fuel power plants do not contribute significantly to air pollution, potentially preventing future administrations from imposing similar regulations under the Clean Air Act. For more than a decade under the Obama and Biden administrations, the EPA had relied on Section 111 of the Clean Air Act as the legal baseline for regulations on U.S. power sector emissions. The EPA no longer believes Section 111 gives it authority to regulate carbon dioxide emissions. If the Trump administration’s proposed changes stand and are upheld in court, a significant portion of federal legislation on the issue would no longer apply.

According to Michelle Bloodworth, president and CEO of America’s Power, the Biden-era rule would have forced coal plants to close, worsening the risk of electricity shortages as electricity demand from data centers, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, and industrial growth increases. Preserving existing coal plants would improve grid reliability, keep electricity prices down, and strengthen U.S. energy security and economic competitiveness.

Rich Nolan, president and CEO of the National Mining Association, indicated that the Trump rule “has averted what would have been a catastrophic collision of unlawful and unworkable Biden-era technology mandates with surging energy demands.” “With today’s repeal, well-operating coal plants are no longer faced with the false choice between commercially unavailable and technically infeasible technologies, fuel-switching, or closure. The administration’s action corrects the egregious misuse of the Clean Air Act as a political tool to end American coal generation and implements the law as Congress intended.”

Environmental groups are likely to challenge the rules, particularly the separate rule that could prevent future administrations from regulating greenhouse gas emissions from power plants. The proposal, expected to be made final next year, follows on EPA’s action earlier this year revoking the endangerment finding that has been the central basis for U.S. action to regulate greenhouse gas emissions under the Obama and Biden administrations.

Background

During the Obama and Biden administrations, the EPA overtly tried to force coal plants out of existence through regulatory authority and Section 111 of the Clean Air Act to cut greenhouse gas emissions. This approach followed Congress’s failure to pass “cap and trade” (or “cap and tax,” as it was called). The strategy’s backbone was the endangerment finding — a 2009 decision by the Obama EPA stating that six greenhouse gases threaten public health and welfare — which the Obama administration made in response to the Supreme Court’s direction in Massachusetts v. EPA. It served as the foundation for federal rules limiting greenhouse gas emissions from motor vehicles and power plants under the two administrations.

In June 2024, the Supreme Court, in Loper Bright v. Raimondo Enterprises, reversed the Chevron Deference doctrine that had allowed the EPA and other federal agencies to redefine the language of federal laws to fit their regulatory agendas. The Trump EPA followed early this year by reversing the Obama-era greenhouse gas endangerment finding, removing the foundation for Obama and Biden efforts to prevent the construction of new coal plants.

The final rule strikes most of the Biden-era 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, which exceeded the EPA’s authority under the Clean Air Act by requiring control technologies (Carbon Capture and Sequestration technologies) that are not adequately demonstrated, effectively forcing plants to retire rather than setting standards they could actually meet. The Trump EPA notes that manipulation in the 2024 rule created inefficient uses of natural gas, adversely impacted the nation’s energy systems, and drove electricity prices up. Consumers have noticed significant electricity cost increases as existing generating units closed and were replaced mostly with new builds of Biden’s politically approved intermittent wind and solar plants.

EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin indicated that Biden-era actions were designed to “suffocate our economy in order to protect the environment,” with the intent to regulate the coal industry “out of existence” and make it “disappear.”

Conclusion

The Trump EPA repealed most of Biden’s 2024 Carbon Pollution Standards, which restrict greenhouse gas emissions from coal and natural gas power plants and are expected to save $310.4 billion over 20 years, lower electricity prices, and increase coal production. The 2024 rule created inefficient uses of natural gas, adversely impacted the nation’s energy systems, and drove up electricity prices. In a separate rule, the Trump EPA is proposing to prevent future administrations from imposing similar regulations under the Clean Air Act by concluding that emissions from fossil-fuel power plants do not contribute significantly to air pollution. Earlier this year, the Trump EPA reversed the Obama-era greenhouse gas endangerment finding, removing the foundation for the Obama and Biden efforts to prevent the building of new coal plants.

In 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency awarded Illinois a $430 million grant to implement programs to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

According to the document, Illinois cut its net greenhouse gas emissions by 32% from 2005 to 2023.

text:
A new report says Illinois has made significant strides in reducing greenhouse gas emissions from power plants such as Illinois has made substantial progress in reducing greenhouse gas emissions in recent years, but it is not yet on track to meet its goal of reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

That's the conclusion of a new Comprehensive Climate Action Plan released this month by the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency.

To reach that goal, the report suggests Illinois will need to enact significant changes across virtually every sector of its economy, including transportation, building construction, manufacturing, agriculture and waste disposal.

"Illinoisans are seeing the extreme heat and storms climate change has brought to our doorstep this summer," Illinois Climate Advisor JC Kibbey said in a statement announcing the report. "We are feeling the high, unpredictable costs of fossil fuel every time we reach for our wallets. This plan shows the great progress we've made on climate and clean energy — and how much more we have left to do."

In 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency awarded Illinois a $430 million grant to implement programs to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. That money came through the federal Climate Pollution Reduction Grant program, which was an element of then-President Joe Biden's signature Inflation Reduction Act.

The Comprehensive Climate Action Plan is intended to provide a roadmap for Illinois to reduce its carbon footprint to as little as 72% below its 2005 baseline. It also outlines two scenarios under which Illinois could virtually eliminate all carbon emissions.

Those would involve a combination of incentive packages and regulatory changes that would affect nearly every sector of the economy. But doing so, the report suggests, would produce $21 billion a year in net economic benefits.

According to the document, Illinois cut its net greenhouse gas emissions by 32% from 2005 to 2023. That was due mainly to a shift in electric generation toward natural gas and renewable sources such as wind and solar power.

The transportation industry also saw significant reductions due to improved fuel efficiency standards and the gradual adoption of electric vehicles.

Those trends are expected to continue into the future as long, the report states, as Illinois adheres to its current policies such as the 2021 Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, which calls for the complete elimination of carbon-emitting power production by 2050, and the state's Electric Vehicle Rebate Program, which offers incentives for lower-income consumers to switch to electric vehicles.

But they will not be enough to reach the goal of net-zero emissions by 2050, according to the report. At best, without any additional policy changes, the report estimates net carbon emissions will only fall to 133 million metric tons by 2050, a 53% reduction below the 2005 baseline.

Path to further reductions

The document outlines a laundry list of additional actions Illinois could take to reduce its carbon footprint even further, starting with providing rebates and other incentives to convert all forms of commercial vehicles, including medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, to electric.

It also proposes new regulations on residential and commercial buildings. Those include adopting clean heat standards that would require a 22% reduction in emissions from natural gas by 2035, offering subsidies to install heat pumps in residential homes, adopting all-electric construction codes for new construction and phasing out gasoline-powered lawn and landscaping equipment by 2035.

It also proposes additional regulations for industrial activities such as requiring net zero emissions from cement production by 2050 and requiring reductions in emissions intensity of cement, glass, iron and steel used in public construction.

The plan also proposes stronger methane monitoring and abatement regulations for landfills and additional incentives for farmers to adopt practices that reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

The report estimates that adopting all the measures outlined in the plan would reduce the state's carbon footprint to 79 million metric tons, or 72% below 2024 levels.

The document also outlines two scenarios for achieving a complete "net zero" footprint by 2050, both requiring high levels of energy efficiency and replacing fossil fuels with electrification or other kinds of renewable fuels.

One plan, called the "moderate efficiency and flexibility" scenario, assumes full electrification of buildings by 2050 with 32% of households using hybrid heat pumps. It also assumes a rapid expansion of electric vehicles.

The "high efficiency and flexibility" scenario places greater emphasis on reducing energy demand. It calls for shifting the focus of new residential development to multifamily buildings instead of single-family homes to reduce heating and cooling loads. It also calls for higher density development and increased reliance on public transportation to reduce the overall number of vehicle miles traveled on roads.

Costs and benefits

The report acknowledges that adopting the policies it outlines would require substantial new investments from the state, private industry and consumers. Those include costs for new infrastructure, vehicles, heat pumps and alternative fuels, to name a few.

But the report says those investments will also yield long-term cost savings from reduced fossil fuel consumption, greater efficiencies, reduced greenhouse gas emissions and improved health and air quality benefits.

It estimates the improvements in air quality alone would lead to between 392 and 631 fewer premature deaths per year. That translates to between $8.8 and $13.8 billion in avoided healthcare costs and increased worker productivity.

"Including the monetized benefits of reduced (greenhouse gas) emissions and health benefits, the total annual net benefit of the Increased State Action scenario reaches $21 billion by 2050," the report concludes.

"Since adoption of the Climate and Equitable Jobs Act, Illinois has been a national leader in addressing carbon emissions, particularly from the energy and transportation sectors," Illinois EPA Director James Jennings said in a statement. "The (Comprehensive Climate Action Plan) builds on these past successes by identifying a path for Illinois to achieve significant reductions in climate change-causing greenhouse gases and meet the state's long term climate goals."

text:
(The Center Square) — New York is leading a coalition of Northeast states in suing the Trump administration to block agreements with two energy companies that would scrap several offshore wind projects, claiming taxpayer money is being used to pay off the companies.

In a pair of lawsuits, filed Tuesday in U.S. District Courts in New York and Maine, James and seven other Democratic attorneys general argue the Trump administration's deals with Bluepoint Wind and Invenergy, would "unlawfully misuse taxpayer dollars and sabotage states’ ability to meet growing energy demands."

The lawsuits allege that the Trump administration struck a deal with the companies to cancel four offshore wind leases and pay the companies nearly $1.4 billion to settle their costs. In exchange, the company agreed to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in oil and gas projects and pledged not to develop any new offshore wind projects, the lawsuit claims.

James, in a statement, blasted the deals and said Americans "are facing increasing energy costs because this administration would rather pay off energy companies than let us build the new power sources we need."

"These illegal backroom deals take money that should have gone toward lowering New Yorkers' bills and hand it to fossil fuel projects in other states, all while our energy demand continues to grow," she said. "At a moment when every available resource should go to keeping the lights on and prices down, this administration is choosing corruption over communities. We will fight until these unlawful deals are struck down."

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, praised the attorneys general for filing the legal challenge and said the two canceled New York projects alone were expected to bring more than $16 billion in investments to the state and create more than 2,800 new jobs. She said the projects planned to connect directly to New York City’s electric grid, "providing a new source of electricity at a time when the state anticipates significant growth in demand."

"The Trump administration's unlawful pay-to-not-play scheme to pressure companies to forego planned offshore wind projects in America is an outrageous abuse of taxpayer dollars that hurts our ability to meet our energy needs, reduce emissions, create good paying jobs, and help secure American energy independence,” she said in a statement.

There was no immediate comment from the Department of Justice about the legal challenges, which were filed with attorneys general from Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Delaware, and Vermont.

President Donald Trump has vowed to end federal support for offshore wind and other clean energy projects as he focuses on boosting fossil fuel production as part of broader efforts to improve the nation’s energy independence.

Trump directed the U.S. Department of Transportation in September to cancel $679 million in federal funding for a dozen infrastructure projects that would support New England Wind and other projects, saying the plans "were not aligned with the goals and priorities of the administration."

In December, the Interior Department halted federal leases for Sunrise and four other large-scale offshore wind projects under construction off New York's coastline, including the Empire Wind 1 project and Sunrise Wind. Those projects have now been allowed to resume construction following federal court rulings.

The federal agency has also pulled the plug on New Jersey's offshore wind projects and clawed back a $12.6 million federal grant for Maine to build the nation's first offshore wind turbine research project.

As cities across the country invest billions of dollars in clean energy and climate infrastructure, a critical question remains largely unanswered: Are these investments working for the people who live closest to these projects?

Researchers from the University of Michigan and Michigan State University received a $1 million grant from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation to launch a first-of-its-kind research initiative to examine how cities can reduce carbon emissions through clean energy investments, while ensuring the communities where these projects are built have a voice in the process and share their benefits.

As cities make major investments in clean energy, understanding who benefits — and who has a say in those decisions — could help communities make the most of the transition while reducing emissions.

The three-year research project, “Decarbonizing the Hood: Conditions, Perceptions, Principles and Evaluation of Equitable Urban Energy Transitions,” brings together researchers, students and community partners to study six urban decarbonization initiatives across Detroit, Chicago and Columbus.

The initiative is led by principal investigator Tony Reames, Tishman Professor of Environmental Justice and director of the School for Environment and Sustainability, or SEAS, Detroit Sustainability Clinic and Urban Energy Justice Lab, and co principal investigator Meghan Wilson, assistant professor of American politics and public policy at Michigan State University’s Department of Political Science.

“This project gives us a unique opportunity to understand how residents participate in planning processes, how benefits and burdens are distributed, and how local governance shapes project outcomes,” Reames said. “Those insights will help us better understand what it takes to advance energy transitions that are not only effective but also equitable.”

text:
Summary

The Province of British Columbia has issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC to expand its existing LNG facility on Tilbury Island in the lower Fraser River in Delta

FortisBC's Phase 2 expansion of the Tilbury Facility would generate billions in economic benefits and drive the Canadian economy forward

Phase 2 would create more than 1,000 construction jobs and as many as 100 long-term jobs once in operation

The expansion supports the growing demand for clean B.C. LNG

The environmental assessment certificate is a key milestone for the project, which would be a major economic and cleaner energy opportunity for B.C.

__________

The Province has issued an environmental assessment certificate to FortisBC to expand its existing LNG facility on Tilbury Island after carefully considering the Environmental Assessment Office’s (EAO) assessment report and recommendations.

This decision will allow FortisBC to move forward with final approvals for a project that could bring billions in economic benefits to British Columbia and create many good-paying jobs. Completion of the environmental assessment was a necessary step before FortisBC makes a final investment decision.

“The Tilbury Phase 2 Expansion project has the potential to deliver significant economic and environmental benefits for B.C., and jobs for British Columbians,” said Adrian Dix, Minister of Energy and Climate Solutions. “After carefully considering the environmental assessment of the project, Environment and Parks Minister Tamara Davidson and I made the decision to issue an environmental assessment certificate, a critical milestone in the authorizations required for this project.”

The Tilbury Phase 2 LNG expansion has been prioritized by the Province as part of B.C.’s Look West strategy for jobs and prosperity. If other required authorizations are received, the project is expected to provide significant economic benefits to B.C. and Canada. The expansion includes the construction of a new 142,400-cubic-metre storage tank and a new liquefication facility capable of producing as much as 2.5 million tonnes of LNG per year, as well as a natural gas receiving facility.

Community benefits of FortisBC’s Tilbury LNG Facility Phase 2

Phase 2 of FortisBC’s Tilbury LNG facility expansion is designed to increase its LNG production capacity, supporting energy resiliency in the Lower Mainland. The expansion also represents an important opportunity to create good-paying jobs, strengthen B.C.’s economy and support greater energy independence.

FortisBC projects capital cost expenditures of $3.1 billion to construct the proposed project over a six-year period. In terms of GDP, FortisBC expects Phase 2 to add $1.7 billion to British Columbia’s GDP during construction and $700 million annually during operations.

The EAO is a neutral regulatory agency that manages environmental assessments of proposed major projects in B.C. to assess potential impacts on people and the environment. The EAO works with and gets input from technical experts, First Nations, companies, the public, local governments, and federal and provincial agencies to assess projects.

The assessment informs the decision by provincial ministers about whether or not to issue an environmental assessment certificate, and what conditions and requirements will be applied to prevent negative impacts and enhance positive impacts.

text:
Montauk Renewables has officially opened its facility in Sampson County, North Carolina, representing a $200 million capital investment in agricultural biogas-to-energy conversion.

The project converts swine waste into renewable natural gas and electricity, whilst producing biochar as a co-product.

The Turkey facility transforms the former Bay Valley Foods Distribution Centre into an agricultural waste management and renewable energy operation.

Montauk has established long-term agreements with more than 80 farming locations across Sampson County, providing access to approximately 415,000 hog spaces targeted for the project's initial phase of operation.

Montauk Renewables specialises in biogas capture and conversion, preventing methane release into the atmosphere whilst converting captured biogas into renewable natural gas (RNG) or electrical power for the grid.

The company operates 14 projects across the United States, with ongoing development in California, Idaho, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. The company has more than 30 years of experience in landfill methane and agricultural biogas systems.

"As of the end of August, we have entered into long-term agreements with over 80 separate farming locations, providing us access to more than 415,000 of the hog spaces we are targeting for our first phase of development," said Sean McClain, Montauk Renewables Chief Executive Officer.

"Farmers are the backbone of the North Carolina economy, and we are thankful to partner with them and Sampson County."

The facility captures methane from swine manure and converts it into renewable energy products. The project also produces biochar, a solid residue that improves soil nutrient and water retention.

Senator Brent Jackson, a Sampson County farmer and leader on agricultural issues in North Carolina's General Assembly, highlighted this dual benefit: "The biochar produced here will also improve nutrient and water retention, supporting healthier soil and stronger crop yields."

The operation addresses a significant intersection of agricultural waste management and renewable energy production.

Swine production generates substantial waste streams across North Carolina, where agriculture represents the state's top industry with annual economic impact exceeding $100 billion.

The state supports approximately 42,000 farms across 8 million acres, with the agricultural sector supporting roughly one in five jobs across the state.

By converting swine waste into energy, the project reduces methane emissions whilst generating revenue from renewable energy products.

Montauk sells both RNG and renewable electricity, taking advantage of environmental attribute premiums available under federal and state policies that incentivise renewable energy production.

The facility's opening signals growing commercial interest in agricultural biogas projects in the United States, particularly in regions with concentrated animal agriculture and established renewable energy incentives.

text:
Monroe County is awarding matching grants to 10 municipalities through the Community Climate Action Fund, an initiative that officials say is designed to preserve natural resources, protect the environment and ensure future livability.

The second phase of the the county’s Climate Action Plan (CAP) is targeting greenhouse gas emissions from county residents, businesses and organizations and is meant to complement Phase I, which focused on emissions from county-owned sites, facilities and operations.

“Climate action is most effective when it starts in local neighborhoods and communities,” County Executive Adam Bello said in a news release. “These grants will help our towns, villages and city of Rochester turn good ideas into real projects that make our communities healthier, more sustainable and more affordable.”

Grants are being awarded to Brighton, Chili, Gates, Hilton, Irondequoit, Penfield, Perinton and Pittsford, along with a combined grant to Greece and the city of Rochester.

County officials made the announcement at the Garnsey Road Arboretum in Perinton, where the town will introduce more trails and create a low-mow grassland that makes room for native species.

“By exploring low-mow and naturalized areas, we can reduce mowing and associated emissions while supporting native habitat and biodiversity,” town Supervisor Jenn Townsend said.

Projects and matching grant amounts:

Brighton: $6,500 (on a $13,000 project) to increase tree cover through the expansion of the community Tree Nursery and the associated Tree Ambassador program.

Chili: $5,300 (on a $10,600 project) to transition park maintenance operations from fossil-fuel-powered equipment to electric equipment to reduce carbon emissions and lessen auditory impacts.

Gates: $10,000 (on a $20,000 project) to initiate a comprehensive stormwater and flood resilience Study to address recurring flooding issues affecting residential neighborhoods, transportation infrastructure and community assets.

Greece and Rochester: $30,000 (on a $60,000 project) to conduct a feasibility/planning study to extend the state route 390 Multi-Use Trail from its current southern terminus at the intersection of Ridgeway Avenue and Latona Road to the Erie Canal and the Empire State Trail in Rochester.

Hilton: $10,000 (on a $25,000 project) to conduct historic window replacement for energy efficiency at the Community Center while maintaining/enhancing historic preservation standards.

Irondequoit: $10,000 (on a $22,500 project) to install a new EV car charger at McAvoy Park.

Penfield: $10,000 (on a $30,000 project) to install a dual port charging station at the Clark House with one standard parking spot and one ADA-compliant spot.

Perinton: $10,000 (on a $32,000 project) to convert approximately seven to eight acres of maintained turf at the Garnsey Arboretum into a low-mow native grassland with defined birdwatching trails.

Pittsford: $10,000 (on a $20,000 project) to plant native trees and establish another pollinator garden to address the loss of trees and provide habitat and support for birds, bees and other wildlife.
